questions.question: What does CDN stand for?

explanation.correct: CDN stands for Content Delivery Network — a system that distributes content to users from geographically distributed servers called edge locations.
explanation.why: A, C, and D are not real AWS or networking terms.

questions.question: Which AWS service is a Content Delivery Network (CDN)?

explanation.correct: Amazon CloudFront is AWS's CDN service that caches and delivers content from edge locations worldwide.
explanation.why: S3 is object storage, Route 53 is DNS, and EC2 is compute.

questions.question: What is an 'edge location' in CloudFront?

options.text: A geographically distributed mini data center that caches content close to users
A private subnet in a VPC

explanation.correct: Edge locations are CloudFront's globally distributed mini data centers where content is cached, separate from AWS Regions and AZs.
explanation.why: Edge locations are distinct from Regions and AZs — they exist specifically for content caching and delivery.

questions.question: What is the default cache TTL for CloudFront?

explanation.correct: CloudFront's default TTL is 24 hours (86,400 seconds). After this period, CloudFront re-fetches the object from the origin on the next request.
explanation.why: You can customize TTL per behavior or per object using Cache-Control headers.

questions.question: What is OAC in CloudFront?

explanation.correct: OAC stands for Origin Access Control — a mechanism that restricts S3 bucket access so only a specific CloudFront distribution can read from it.
explanation.why: OAC replaced the older OAI (Origin Access Identity) and is the current recommended method.

questions.question: What port does Route 53 use, which is reflected in its name?

explanation.correct: Route 53 is named after port 53, the standard port for DNS (Domain Name System) traffic.
explanation.why: Port 80 is HTTP, 443 is HTTPS, and 22 is SSH.

questions.question: What is a hosted zone in Route 53?

options.text: An EC2 instance running a DNS server
A container for DNS records for a specific domain
A CloudFront distribution with a custom domain
A VPC with DNS resolution enabled

explanation.correct: A hosted zone is a container that holds DNS records for a domain (e.g., myshop.com). Route 53 uses it to route traffic for that domain and its subdomains.
explanation.why: Hosted zones are entirely managed by Route 53 — no EC2 DNS servers needed.

questions.question: How many name servers does Route 53 assign to a hosted zone?

explanation.correct: Route 53 assigns four name servers to every hosted zone for high availability and redundancy.
explanation.why: Using four name servers ensures DNS resolution continues even if one or two are temporarily unavailable.

questions.question: What does Boto3 refer to?

options.text: The official AWS SDK for Python
A Python framework for building serverless apps
An AWS service for running Python code

explanation.correct: Boto3 is the official AWS SDK for Python, allowing developers to interact with AWS services programmatically from Python code.
explanation.why: AWS CLI is a separate command-line tool. Lambda runs Python code serverlessly. There is no 'AWS CLI for Python' — CLI and SDK are different tools.

questions.question: Which command installs the AWS CLI configuration (credentials, region)?

explanation.correct: 'aws configure' is the CLI command that prompts you to enter your Access Key ID, Secret Access Key, default region, and output format.
explanation.why: 'aws setup' and 'boto3 configure' do not exist. 'pip install awscli' installs the CLI tool but does not configure credentials.

questions.question: Where are AMI IDs valid?

options.text: Only within a single AWS Account
Only within a specific AWS Region
Only within a specific Availability Zone

explanation.correct: AMI IDs are region-specific. The same operating system image has a different AMI ID in each AWS region. Using an AMI ID from one region in another will result in an error.
explanation.why: This is a common beginner mistake — always look up the AMI ID in the AWS Console for the specific region you are deploying to.

questions.question: What is the recommended replacement for Origin Access Identity (OAI) in CloudFront?

explanation.correct: Origin Access Control (OAC) is the recommended replacement for OAI. It supports all S3 regions, SSE-KMS encryption, and dynamic requests.
explanation.why: OAI is the older legacy method. OAC provides all the same functionality plus additional features.

questions.question: Which DNS record type can be used at the apex (root) domain in Route 53?

explanation.correct: Alias A records are an AWS-specific extension that can be used at the apex domain (e.g., myshop.com, not just www.myshop.com). CNAME records cannot be used at the apex domain per DNS standards.
explanation.why: Using a CNAME at the apex domain violates RFC 1034 and would break other DNS records like MX for email.

questions.question: In which AWS region must ACM (SSL) certificates be requested for use with CloudFront?

options.text: The same region as the S3 origin
Any region — CloudFront accepts certificates from all regions

explanation.correct: ACM certificates for CloudFront must be created in us-east-1 (N. Virginia), regardless of where your users are or where your origin is located. This is a CloudFront requirement.
explanation.why: CloudFront is a global service managed from us-east-1. It only reads ACM certificates from that region.

questions.question: What happens when a CloudFront edge location receives a request for content it does not have cached?

options.text: It returns a 404 error to the user
It fetches the content from the origin, caches it locally, and delivers it to the user
It redirects the user directly to the S3 URL
It waits until the cache is refreshed on the next scheduled TTL cycle

explanation.correct: A cache miss triggers CloudFront to fetch the object from the origin (e.g., S3), store a copy at the edge location, then serve it to the requesting user. Future requests for the same object at that edge will be cache hits.
explanation.why: CloudFront never returns 404 just because content isn't cached — it always goes to the origin as a fallback.

questions.question: Which Route 53 routing policy distributes traffic between multiple targets based on percentage?

explanation.correct: Weighted routing lets you assign percentage weights to different targets, such as 90% to version 1 and 10% to version 2. This is commonly used for A/B testing and canary deployments.
explanation.why: Latency routes to the lowest-latency region. Failover handles active/passive. Simple has a single destination.

questions.question: Where does Boto3 look for AWS credentials when you run a Python script locally?

options.text: The ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.aws/config files (set by aws configure)

explanation.correct: When you run 'aws configure', credentials are stored in ~/.aws/credentials and region/output settings in ~/.aws/config. Boto3 reads from these files automatically when running locally.
explanation.why: EC2 metadata endpoint is used when running inside an EC2 instance with an IAM role attached — not for local scripts.

questions.question: A company wants to automatically route traffic to a backup site if the primary site fails. Which Route 53 routing policy should they use?

explanation.correct: Failover routing is designed for active-passive setups. Route 53 sends traffic to the primary resource. If a health check detects the primary is down, traffic is automatically rerouted to the secondary (failover) resource.
explanation.why: Weighted splits traffic on purpose. Latency routes by speed. Multivalue returns multiple IPs but does not handle failover logic.

questions.question: What is a Boto3 'resource' interface vs a 'client' interface?

options.text: Resource is for EC2 only; client is for all other services
Resource is a high-level object-oriented interface; client is a low-level API-mapped interface
Client returns JSON; resource returns XML
They are identical — just two names for the same thing

explanation.correct: Boto3 Resource provides a high-level, object-oriented interface (e.g., instance.start(), bucket.upload_file()). Client provides a 1-to-1 mapping with the AWS API and returns raw Python dicts. Not all services have a Resource interface.
explanation.why: Both interfaces ultimately call the same AWS APIs — they differ in abstraction level and ease of use.

questions.question: How does an Alias A record in Route 53 differ from a standard A record?

options.text: An Alias record stores the IPv6 address; a standard A record stores IPv4
An Alias record points to an AWS resource (like CloudFront) using its DNS name; a standard A record points to a static IPv4 address
An Alias record is only for private hosted zones
An Alias record requires an ACM certificate

explanation.correct: An Alias A record maps a domain to an AWS resource's DNS name (e.g., a CloudFront distribution domain). Route 53 automatically resolves that to the correct IP. This works at the apex domain and is free for AWS resource targets.
explanation.why: Alias records are AWS-specific and exist precisely to point to AWS-managed resources whose IPs can change dynamically.

questions.question: Your S3 bucket has no public access and your OAC is configured. A user tries to access the website using the direct S3 static website URL. What response do they get?

options.text: 301 Redirect — they are redirected to CloudFront
403 Forbidden — S3 denies the request because no public access is allowed
404 Not Found — S3 does not recognize the URL

explanation.correct: With all public access blocked and no public bucket policy, any direct request to S3 — including the static website URL — returns 403 Forbidden. Only CloudFront (via OAC) is permitted to read from the bucket.
explanation.why: This is the desired outcome — the S3 URL is intentionally inaccessible; the CloudFront URL is the only way to reach the content.

questions.question: Which of the following is a best practice for authenticating Boto3 scripts running on an EC2 instance?

options.text: Hardcode the Access Key ID and Secret Key in the Python script
Store credentials in a plain text file in the project directory
Attach an IAM role to the EC2 instance — no credentials needed in the code
Use the root account credentials for maximum permissions

explanation.correct: The best practice is to attach an IAM role to the EC2 instance with the minimum required permissions. Boto3 automatically retrieves temporary credentials from the EC2 instance metadata service — no access keys needed in code.
explanation.why: Hardcoded credentials, plain text files, and root account usage are all serious security antipatterns that violate AWS security best practices.

questions.question: A team uses CloudFront in front of their S3 website. They updated their homepage but users still see the old version hours later. What is the fastest way to force CloudFront to serve the new version?

options.text: Delete and recreate the CloudFront distribution
Wait for the TTL to expire naturally
Create a CloudFront cache invalidation for the updated file path

explanation.correct: A cache invalidation tells CloudFront to remove a specific file (or wildcard path) from all edge location caches immediately, forcing edge locations to fetch the updated version from the origin on the next request.
explanation.why: Deleting the distribution would break the website. Waiting for TTL could take up to 24 hours. Changing the bucket region has no effect on CloudFront's cached copies.

questions.question: Which Route 53 routing policy automatically routes users to the lowest-latency AWS region?

explanation.correct: Latency-based routing measures the network latency between the user and each configured AWS region, then routes the request to the region with the lowest latency. This is different from geolocation routing, which routes by country/continent regardless of actual latency.
explanation.why: Geolocation routes by country/continent. Weighted routes by percentage. Geoproximity routes by distance with an adjustable bias offset.

questions.question: A developer needs their Python application (running on EC2) to upload files to S3, create SQS messages, and query DynamoDB. How should they authenticate the application?

options.text: Hardcode access keys in environment variables
Create an IAM user and store credentials in the code
Attach an IAM role to the EC2 instance with permissions for S3, SQS, and DynamoDB
Use the root account credentials in the config file

explanation.correct: Attach an IAM role to the EC2 instance with only the required permissions (principle of least privilege). The application uses Boto3 with no credentials in code — Boto3 automatically retrieves temporary credentials from the instance metadata service.
explanation.why: Hardcoded credentials and root account access are severe security violations. IAM roles with temporary credentials are the AWS-recommended pattern for applications running on EC2.

questions.question: Which of the following Route 53 record types is AWS-specific and does not exist in standard DNS?

explanation.correct: Alias records are an AWS Route 53 extension that doesn't exist in standard DNS. They allow DNS-level mapping to AWS resources (CloudFront, ELB, S3) and support apex domain usage — which standard CNAME records prohibit.
explanation.why: A, CNAME, and MX are all standard DNS record types defined in RFCs. Alias records are Route 53-specific.

questions.question: An application needs to serve 80% of users with version 1 of an API and 20% with version 2 for testing. Which Route 53 routing policy achieves this?

explanation.correct: Weighted routing allows exact percentage splits between multiple endpoints. Setting weight 80 on version 1 and weight 20 on version 2 achieves an 80/20 traffic split — ideal for canary deployments and A/B testing.
explanation.why: Latency routes by speed, not percentage. Failover is for disaster recovery. Multivalue returns multiple IPs but doesn't split by percentage.

questions.question: What will happen if you use a CNAME record for the root domain 'myshop.com' in Route 53?

options.text: It works the same as an Alias record
Route 53 will not allow it — CNAME at apex domain is not permitted
It works but costs more than an Alias record
It works but only for HTTP, not HTTPS

explanation.correct: CNAME records cannot be created at the apex (root) domain per the DNS standard (RFC 1034). A CNAME at the root would conflict with other required records like SOA and NS. Route 53 enforces this restriction. Use an Alias A record instead.
explanation.why: This is a critical exam topic — always use Alias records for apex domains pointing to AWS resources.

questions.question: A company uses CloudFront with S3 as origin. They want to ensure users only access the site over HTTPS and all HTTP requests are redirected. Where is this configured?

options.text: In the S3 bucket CORS policy
In the CloudFront distribution behavior settings under 'Viewer Protocol Policy'

explanation.correct: CloudFront behaviors have a 'Viewer Protocol Policy' setting that controls how viewers communicate with CloudFront. Setting it to 'Redirect HTTP to HTTPS' ensures all HTTP requests are automatically redirected to HTTPS at the edge.
explanation.why: S3, Route 53, and ACM do not control protocol enforcement at the CloudFront level. This is a CloudFront distribution configuration.

questions.question: A Boto3 script to launch EC2 fails with 'InvalidAMIID.NotFound' even though the AMI ID looks correct. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The IAM user does not have EC2 permissions
The AMI ID is from a different AWS region than where the script is deploying
The AMI has been deregistered by AWS automatically

explanation.correct: AMI IDs are region-specific. If you copy an AMI ID from us-east-1 and use it in a script deploying to ap-south-1, you get InvalidAMIID.NotFound. Always find the correct AMI ID for your target region.
explanation.why: Missing IAM permissions would give an Access Denied error. Boto3 installation issues cause import errors, not AMI errors. AWS does not auto-deregister AMIs.
